title: The Universe and Earth's Place in It
bigQuestion: How can we know the age, size and history of a universe we can never visit?

story.title: The Star That Changed the Map of Everything
story.kicker: One faint dot on a glass photographic plate pushed the edge of the known universe out by millions of light-years.
paragraphs: In October 1923, Edwin Hubble sat at the eyepiece of the largest telescope on Earth. The Hooker telescope on Mount Wilson, above Los Angeles, had a mirror 2.5 meters across. Hubble aimed it at a fuzzy smudge called the Andromeda nebula. He exposed a glass plate for most of a night. Astronomers had argued for years about what that smudge was. Some said it was a cloud of gas inside our own Milky Way. Others said it was a separate galaxy, an island of stars unimaginably far away.

On the plate, Hubble found a faint point of light that had not been there before. He marked it with an N, for nova, a star that flares up once. Then he checked older plates of the same spot. The star had not flared once. It brightened and dimmed again and again, on a steady rhythm of about a month. Hubble crossed out the N and wrote VAR! in red. This was a Cepheid variable, a kind of star whose rhythm reveals its true brightness.

A decade earlier, Henrietta Leavitt at Harvard had found the rule: the slower a Cepheid blinks, the brighter it truly is. Compare true brightness to how dim it looks, and you get its distance. Hubble did the arithmetic. His answer was about 900,000 light-years. That was far beyond any estimate of the Milky Way's size. Later measurements pushed the number to about 2.5 million light-years, but the conclusion held.

Andromeda was not a nebula. It was a galaxy, a whole other Milky Way. The universe was suddenly much bigger than anyone had known, and full of galaxies. Hubble had not guessed this. He had measured it, from one blinking star on a piece of glass. Within a few years he would use the same tools to show that those galaxies were rushing away from each other, and the universe itself was expanding.
story.think: Hubble first labeled the star wrong, then fixed it by checking old plates. Why does science depend on records that let someone check a claim later?

lessons.title: Barcodes in Starlight
lessons.mainIdea: Spread starlight into a spectrum and its dark lines tell you which elements the star holds.
reading: Hold a glass prism in sunlight and a rainbow spreads across the wall. Isaac Newton did this in the 1660s and showed that white light is a mix of every color. In 1814 a German lens maker, Joseph von Fraunhofer, looked closer. He built a tool that spread sunlight very wide and saw hundreds of thin dark lines cutting across the rainbow. They were always in the same places. No one knew what they meant.

The answer came in 1859. Gustav Kirchhoff and Robert Bunsen heated pure *elements* in a flame and passed the light through a prism. Each element glowed in its own set of bright lines, like a barcode. Sodium always made two yellow lines. Hydrogen made a red line, a blue-green line and more. When light from a hot source passed through cooler gas of that element, the gas soaked up those same colors, leaving dark *absorption lines* at the same places.

That meant the dark lines in the sun's *spectrum* were a list of ingredients. The sun's outer gas was absorbing light at the barcode of hydrogen, sodium, iron and more. In 1868 astronomers found a yellow line in the sun that matched no known element. They named the unknown element helium, after the Greek word for sun. Helium was not found on Earth until 1895. A star 150 million kilometers away had shown chemists an element before they found it under their feet.

Every star we can see sends us this kind of message. A spectrum tells us what a star is made of, how hot it is, and, as you will see later, whether it is moving toward us or away. We cannot scoop up a piece of a star. We do not have to. The light already carries the evidence.

words.d: light spread out into its colors, from red to violet, so each wavelength can be seen separately
a dark gap in a spectrum where a gas has soaked up one exact color of light
a pure substance made of one kind of atom, such as hydrogen or iron

look.title: Two Spectra Side by Side
look.text: Picture two strips of rainbow on a screen. The top strip comes from a lamp full of glowing sodium gas in the lab: two bright yellow lines close together. The bottom strip is sunlight: a full rainbow with two thin dark lines in exactly the same yellow spot.
look.prompt: What does the match between the bright lab lines and the dark sun lines tell you about the sun's outer layers?

check.q: What are the dark lines in the sun's spectrum?
choices: Colors absorbed by gases in the sun's outer layers
Shadows of sunspots
Dust in Earth's air blocking light
Gaps where the prism is scratched
check.why: Kirchhoff and Bunsen showed that a cooler gas absorbs the same exact colors it would glow with. The lines are the sun's own gases soaking up light.

check.q: Helium was named after the sun because:
choices: It was the most common gas on Earth
Its spectral line was seen in sunlight before the element was found on Earth
It made the sun's light yellow
Newton discovered it with his prism
check.why: In 1868 a yellow line in the sun's spectrum matched no known element. Helium was not found on Earth until 1895.

check.q: A distant star shows the barcode of iron in its spectrum. What can you conclude?
choices: The star is made only of iron
The star is cooler than the sun
The star's outer gas contains iron
The star is moving away from us
check.why: Absorption lines show which elements are present in the gas the light passed through. They do not by themselves show the amount or the motion.

lessons.title: Bigger Eyes on the Sky
lessons.mainIdea: Each larger telescope gathered more light and revealed objects no one had seen, and each one changed what people believed about the sky.
reading: In 1608 a Dutch spectacle maker asked for a patent on a tube with two lenses that made far things look near. Word spread fast. By late 1609 Galileo Galilei in Italy had built his own and pointed it up. He saw mountains and craters on the moon, which was supposed to be a perfect smooth sphere. He saw four small lights moving around Jupiter, night after night. Here were moons orbiting something other than Earth. Not everything circled us.

Galileo's tube was a *refracting telescope*: a lens bends light to a focus. Big lenses sag under their own weight, so there is a limit. In 1668 Isaac Newton built a *reflecting telescope* that uses a curved mirror instead. A mirror can be supported from behind, so it can be made huge. Almost every large telescope since has been a reflector.

Why does size matter? A telescope is a bucket for light. A mirror twice as wide has four times the area and catches four times the light. Faint, far things become visible. The 2.5-meter Hooker telescope of 1917 let Hubble find Cepheids in Andromeda. The 5-meter Hale telescope of 1948 reached much farther. Today mirrors on mountaintops are 8 to 10 meters across, and several 30-meter-class telescopes are being built.

The next step was to leave the air behind. Earth's atmosphere blurs and blocks light, which is why stars twinkle. The Hubble Space Telescope, launched in 1990 with a 2.4-meter mirror, sees sharper than much bigger telescopes on the ground. The James Webb Space Telescope, launched in December 2021, has a 6.5-meter mirror and sees infrared light from the earliest galaxies. Chicago has its own piece of this history: the University of Chicago's Yerkes Observatory in Wisconsin, opened in 1897, holds the largest refracting lens ever put to use, about 1 meter across.

words.d: a telescope that uses a lens to bend light to a focus
a telescope that uses a curved mirror to gather and focus light
how much light a telescope collects, which grows with the area of its lens or mirror

look.title: Galileo Reports on Jupiter, 1610
look.text: In his short book The Starry Messenger, Galileo described watching Jupiter in January 1610. He wrote that he saw three, then four, small stars near the planet that changed position from night to night but never left it, and he concluded that they were moons circling Jupiter just as the moon circles Earth.
look.cite: Galileo Galilei, Sidereus Nuncius (The Starry Messenger), 1610
look.prompt: Why did moons orbiting Jupiter matter so much to the argument about whether Earth was the center of everything?

check.q: Why are almost all large modern telescopes reflectors rather than refractors?
choices: Mirrors make brighter colors
A big mirror can be supported from behind, while a big lens sags
Lenses were banned after Galileo
Reflectors are cheaper to ship into space
check.why: A lens can only be held at its edge and bends under its own weight. A mirror can be braced across its whole back, so it can be made much larger.

check.q: A telescope mirror is made three times wider. How does the light it gathers change?
choices: It triples
It stays the same
It grows about nine times
It doubles
check.why: Light-gathering power depends on area, and area grows with the square of the width. Three times wider means nine times the area.

check.q: Why can the 2.4-meter Hubble Space Telescope see finer detail than a 5-meter telescope on a mountain?
choices: Its mirror is made of gold
It is closer to the stars
It orbits faster than Earth turns
It is above the atmosphere that blurs light
check.why: Earth's air bends and blurs starlight, which is why stars twinkle. In orbit there is no air in the way, so images are much sharper.

lessons.title: A Ruler Made of Blinking Stars
lessons.mainIdea: Cepheid variables blink on a rhythm tied to their true brightness, so comparing true to apparent brightness gives their distance.
reading: How far away is a star? For the nearest ones there is a trick you can test with your own thumb. Hold your thumb out and close one eye, then the other. Your thumb seems to jump against the background. That jump is *parallax*. Astronomers watch a nearby star from opposite sides of Earth's orbit, six months apart, and measure its tiny jump against far stars. In 1838 Friedrich Bessel used this to get the first star distance. But beyond a few thousand light-years the jump is too small to measure.

For farther stars, astronomers needed a standard candle: an object whose true brightness they knew. Then the rule is simple. Light spreads out, so a lamp twice as far away looks one quarter as bright. Know the true brightness, measure how bright it looks, and the distance follows. The problem was finding a kind of star whose true brightness could be known.

Henrietta Leavitt found one. She worked at Harvard College Observatory measuring stars on photographic plates. She studied *Cepheid variables*, stars that swell and shrink, brightening and dimming on a regular *period* of days to weeks. She focused on Cepheids in the Small Magellanic Cloud, all about the same distance from us. In 1912 she reported a clear pattern: the longer the period, the brighter the star. A slow blinker is a bright star. A fast blinker is a dim one.

Time a Cepheid's rhythm and you know its true *luminosity*. Compare that to its apparent brightness and you have its distance, even millions of light-years away. This is the tool Hubble used on Andromeda. It is still one rung on the ladder astronomers climb to measure the universe, checked against parallax at the bottom and against exploding stars at the top.

words.d: the apparent shift of a nearby object against a far background when you look from two places
a star that brightens and dims on a regular cycle whose length reveals its true brightness
the time one full cycle takes, such as one brightening and dimming of a variable star
the true total brightness of a star, how much light it actually gives off

look.title: Leavitt's Pattern, 1912
look.text: Reporting on 25 variable stars in the Small Magellanic Cloud, Leavitt noted that a remarkable relationship stood out between how bright the stars were and how long their cycles took: the brighter variables had the longer periods. Because the stars were all at nearly the same distance, she reasoned that the pattern reflected their real light output, not just their distance from us.
look.cite: Henrietta Leavitt, Harvard College Observatory Circular 173, 1912
look.prompt: Why was it important that all 25 stars were at about the same distance from Earth?

check.q: Two Cepheids look equally bright in the sky. One blinks every 3 days, the other every 30 days. Which is farther away?
choices: They are the same distance
The 3-day star
The 30-day star
It cannot be known from this
check.why: The slow 30-day star is truly much brighter. To look only as bright as the dim fast star, it must be much farther away.

check.q: Why does parallax fail for very distant stars?
choices: Distant stars do not move
Distant stars are too dim to photograph
Earth's orbit is too fast
The shift becomes too tiny to measure
check.why: Parallax shrinks as distance grows. Beyond a few thousand light-years the apparent jump is smaller than instruments can detect.

check.q: A lamp is moved from 10 meters to 20 meters away. How bright does it look now?
choices: One quarter as bright
Half as bright
The same
One eighth as bright
check.why: Light spreads over an area that grows with the square of the distance. Twice as far means one quarter the brightness.

sections.title: How the Sun and Stars Work

lessons.title: The Sun's Furnace
lessons.mainIdea: The sun shines because hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium in its core, turning a little mass into a great deal of energy.
reading: The sun has been shining for about 4.6 billion years. Nothing burning like wood or coal could last that long. In the 1800s scientists tried to explain the sun's heat with slow shrinking under gravity, but that gave only tens of millions of years, far less than geologists needed for Earth's rocks. The energy source had to be something new.

The answer is *nuclear fusion*. In the sun's *core* the temperature is about 15 million degrees Celsius and the pressure is enormous. Atoms there are stripped into bare nuclei and electrons, a state called *plasma*. Hydrogen nuclei slam together so hard that they stick. Through a series of steps, four hydrogen nuclei become one helium nucleus. The helium has slightly less mass than the four hydrogens, about 0.7 percent less. That missing mass becomes energy, following Einstein's rule that energy equals mass times the speed of light squared.

A tiny bit of mass makes a huge amount of energy, because the speed of light is so large. The sun converts roughly 4 million tons of mass into energy every second. It has enough hydrogen to keep doing this for billions more years. The energy takes a very long time to work its way out through the dense inner layers. Then it crosses the 150 million kilometers to Earth in about 8 minutes as light.

Arthur Eddington suggested in 1920 that fusion powered the stars. Hans Bethe worked out the detailed steps in 1939. The evidence includes the sun's spectrum, its mass and size, its steady output, and neutrinos, ghostly particles produced in the core that detectors deep underground now catch. The furnace idea explains the sun's age, its energy and its makeup all at once.

words.d: the joining of light atomic nuclei into a heavier nucleus, releasing energy
the hot, dense center of a star where fusion happens
gas so hot that its atoms have split into nuclei and free electrons

look.title: What the Sun Is Made Of
look.prompt: The sun turns hydrogen into helium. Over billions of years, which way should these two numbers shift, and why?

check.q: Where does the sun's energy come from?
choices: Hydrogen nuclei fusing into helium in the core
Burning of hydrogen gas with oxygen
The sun slowly shrinking under gravity
Sunlight reflected from the planets
check.why: Fusion in the core converts a small fraction of mass into energy. Burning and shrinking cannot supply energy for billions of years.

check.q: Four hydrogen nuclei fuse into one helium nucleus. What happens to the total mass?
choices: It increases slightly
It decreases slightly and the difference becomes energy
It stays exactly the same
It doubles
check.why: The helium nucleus has about 0.7 percent less mass than the four hydrogen nuclei. That lost mass is released as energy.

check.q: Why did the 1800s idea of the sun shrinking under gravity fail?
choices: The sun is not affected by gravity
The sun is getting larger, not smaller
It gave far too short a lifetime for the sun
Shrinking makes things colder
check.why: Gravitational shrinking could power the sun for only tens of millions of years, but Earth's rocks showed the sun had been shining far longer.

lessons.title: How a Star Lives and Dies
lessons.mainIdea: A star's mass decides how fast it burns its fuel and whether it ends as a white dwarf or in a supernova.
reading: Stars are born inside cold clouds of gas and dust when gravity pulls a clump together. The clump heats as it squeezes. When the core reaches about 10 million degrees, fusion begins and a star is born. For most of its life, a star fuses hydrogen into helium in its core. Astronomers call this stage the *main sequence*. The sun has been on the main sequence for about 4.6 billion years and has about 5 billion years to go.

Mass is destiny. A star with more mass has stronger gravity crushing its core, which makes fusion run hotter and faster. So big stars burn through fuel quickly and shine for only millions of years, while small stars sip fuel for hundreds of billions. It seems backward, but a campfire with a huge pile of wood can burn out sooner if it blazes hard enough.

When the core's hydrogen runs out, the star changes. The core shrinks and heats, the outer layers swell, and the star becomes a *red giant*, cooler but far larger. The sun's giant stage will swallow Mercury and Venus. A sun-sized star then fuses helium into carbon, puffs off its outer layers as a glowing shell, and leaves behind a hot, dense *white dwarf* the size of Earth that cools for ages.

A star more than about eight times the sun's mass goes further. Its core fuses heavier and heavier elements up to iron. Iron gives back no energy when fused, so the core collapses in a fraction of a second. The outer layers rebound in a *supernova*, an explosion that can outshine a whole galaxy for weeks. What remains is a neutron star or a black hole. Chinese astronomers recorded such an explosion in 1054; its remains, the Crab Nebula, are still expanding today.

words.d: the long, stable stage of a star's life when it fuses hydrogen in its core
a swollen, cooler star that forms after a star's core hydrogen runs out
the small, hot, dense leftover core of a sun-like star
the explosion of a massive star at the end of its life

look.title: Two Stars, Same Birthday
look.text: Imagine two stars born from the same cloud on the same day. One has half the mass of the sun. The other has twenty times the sun's mass. The big one shines thousands of times brighter, blue-white and fierce. The small one glows a dim orange-red.
look.prompt: Which star will still be shining a billion years from now, and what does the other one's fate look like?

check.q: Which statement about star mass is correct?
choices: Massive stars live longer because they have more fuel
Massive stars burn faster and live shorter lives
All stars live about 10 billion years
Small stars are hotter than large ones
check.why: Stronger gravity in a massive star makes its core hotter, so fusion runs much faster. The extra fuel is used up far more quickly.

check.q: What will the sun become at the very end of its life?
choices: A black hole
A neutron star
A white dwarf
A new main-sequence star
check.why: The sun is too light to explode. After its red giant stage it will shed its outer layers and leave a white dwarf.

check.q: Why does a massive star's core collapse once it makes iron?
choices: Iron is too heavy to stay in the core
Iron melts the core
Iron makes the star spin too fast
Fusing iron gives no energy, so nothing holds up the core
check.why: Fusion of lighter elements releases energy that pushes outward against gravity. Iron fusion takes energy instead, so the push stops and gravity wins.

lessons.title: Where Your Atoms Came From
lessons.mainIdea: Hydrogen and helium came from the early universe; nearly every heavier atom in your body was made inside stars.
reading: Look at your hand. The carbon in your skin, the calcium in your bones and the iron in your blood are atoms with a history. Each one was made somewhere, and the evidence from spectra and from nuclear physics tells a consistent story. The early universe made only the lightest elements. Everything heavier was cooked in stars.

In its first few minutes the universe was hot and dense enough for fusion everywhere. It made hydrogen, helium and a trace of lithium, then cooled too much to go further. That is why the oldest stars we find are almost pure hydrogen and helium. It is also why those two elements still make up about 98 percent of ordinary matter today.

Stars are the factories for the rest. Through their lives they fuse hydrogen into helium, helium into carbon and oxygen, and in massive stars onward to silicon and iron. Elements heavier than iron, such as gold and uranium, need an even more violent setting: the flood of neutrons in a supernova or the collision of two neutron stars. In 2017 astronomers watched such a collision and saw the spectral signs of freshly made heavy elements in its glow.

Dying stars scatter their atoms back into space. New clouds form from the enriched gas, and new stars and planets form from those clouds. Our sun is at least a second-generation star, born from a cloud already seeded with the ashes of earlier ones. Every heavy atom on Earth spent time inside a star that died before the sun was born. Carl Sagan put it plainly: we are made of star stuff.

words.d: the crushed, city-sized remnant left by some supernovas, made mostly of neutrons
the third-lightest element, one of the few made in the early universe
a star formed from gas that earlier stars had already enriched with heavier elements

look.title: Old Star, Young Star
look.text: Astronomers compare two spectra. The first star's light shows only hydrogen and helium lines, with almost nothing else. The second star's light shows strong lines of iron, calcium, carbon and oxygen along with hydrogen and helium.
look.prompt: Which star probably formed earlier in the universe's history, and what does the difference tell you about where heavy elements come from?

check.q: Which elements did the early universe make in its first few minutes?
choices: Iron and gold
Carbon and oxygen
Hydrogen, helium and a trace of lithium
Every element up to uranium
check.why: The universe cooled too fast for fusion to go beyond the lightest elements. Heavier atoms had to wait for stars.

check.q: Where is most of the iron in your blood thought to have been made?
choices: In Earth's core
In the sun's core
In the Big Bang
Inside massive stars that died before the sun formed
check.why: Iron forms in the cores of massive stars and is scattered when they explode. The sun formed from a cloud that already held such iron.

check.q: Why do the oldest stars contain almost no heavy elements?
choices: They formed before stars had made and scattered heavy elements
Heavy elements sink out of old stars
Old stars burn their heavy elements away
Heavy elements form only on planets
check.why: The gas available when the first stars formed was nearly pure hydrogen and helium. Heavy elements were made later inside stars.

lessons.title: Stretched Light and Fleeing Galaxies
lessons.mainIdea: Galaxies' spectra are shifted toward red, and the farther the galaxy, the bigger the shift: the universe is expanding.
reading: Stand by a road as a car honks past. The horn sounds higher as the car approaches and lower as it pulls away. The sound waves are squeezed in front and stretched behind. This is the *Doppler effect*, and it works for light too. Light from a source moving away is stretched to longer, redder wavelengths. Light from a source moving toward you is squeezed toward blue.

The barcode lines in a spectrum make this measurable. Hydrogen's lines are always in the same places in a lab. If a galaxy's hydrogen lines all sit a little toward the red end, the galaxy is moving away. The size of the shift gives the speed. Astronomers call this *redshift*. Starting in 1912, Vesto Slipher in Arizona measured spirals and found that almost all were redshifted, some racing away at over 1,000 kilometers per second.

Hubble combined Slipher's speeds with his own Cepheid distances. In 1929 he reported a simple pattern: the farther a galaxy is, the faster it recedes. Twice the distance, twice the speed. This is now called *Hubble's law*. It is exactly what you would see if space itself were stretching, carrying galaxies apart like raisins in rising dough. From every raisin, the others move away, and the far ones fastest.

This was not what most scientists expected. Even Einstein had assumed a universe that stayed the same size. The data said otherwise. Run the expansion backward and everything was once packed together, hot and dense. Hubble's plot of speed against distance was the first strong evidence for a beginning. Later astronomers named that beginning the Big Bang.

words.d: the change in wavelength of sound or light when the source moves toward or away from you
the stretching of a light source's spectral lines toward longer wavelengths because it is moving away
the pattern that a galaxy's speed away from us grows in proportion to its distance

look.title: Hubble's Result, 1929
look.text: In a short paper for the National Academy of Sciences, Hubble reported distances and velocities for two dozen galaxies. He wrote that the data showed a roughly linear relation between velocity and distance among the nebulae, and he noted that the relation was a striking feature that might have real meaning for how the universe behaves on the largest scales.
look.cite: Edwin Hubble, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 1929
look.prompt: Hubble had only about two dozen galaxies and rough distances. What would make you more confident in the pattern he found?

check.q: A galaxy's hydrogen lines appear shifted toward the red end of the spectrum. What does this mean?
choices: The galaxy is cooler than the sun
The galaxy is moving away from us
The galaxy contains a lot of red stars
The galaxy is spinning fast
check.why: Light from a source moving away is stretched to longer, redder wavelengths. The lines shift as a group, which is how astronomers know it is motion, not color.

check.q: According to Hubble's law, a galaxy twice as far away as another should:
choices: Be moving toward us
Be moving away at the same speed
Be moving away about twice as fast
Be moving away about half as fast
check.why: Hubble found that recession speed grows in proportion to distance. That is what uniform stretching of space produces.

check.q: Why did Hubble's finding point to a beginning of the universe?
choices: Because galaxies were being destroyed
Because the sun was found to be young
Because redshift means light gets old
Because running the expansion backward puts everything together at one time
check.why: If galaxies are flying apart now, they were closer in the past. Tracing back leads to a hot, dense early state.

lessons.title: The Glow Left Over
lessons.mainIdea: A faint microwave glow from every direction is the cooled light of the hot early universe, predicted before it was found.
reading: If the universe began hot and dense, the early glow should still be around. In 1948 physicists working with George Gamow predicted it. The early universe was a hot fog of plasma that light could not cross. About 380,000 years after the beginning, it cooled enough for atoms to form and the fog cleared. The light released then has been traveling ever since, stretched by expansion from a fierce orange glow to faint microwaves just a few degrees above absolute zero.

The prediction was mostly forgotten. Then in 1964 Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson at Bell Labs in New Jersey were testing a large horn-shaped radio antenna. They heard a steady hiss they could not remove. It came from every direction, day and night, all year. They cleaned out pigeon droppings and checked every wire. The hiss stayed. Physicists nearby recognized it: this was the leftover glow, now called the *cosmic microwave background*.

Its temperature is about 2.7 *kelvin*, meaning 2.7 degrees above *absolute zero*. It fills the whole sky almost perfectly evenly. In the 1990s the COBE satellite measured its spectrum and found the exact shape expected from a hot, glowing body that had cooled by stretching. COBE and later satellites also mapped tiny ripples, differences of a few parts in 100,000. Those faint ripples were the seeds that gravity grew into galaxies.

The microwave background is the strongest evidence for the Big Bang. It was predicted in detail before anyone looked, then found by accident by people who were not looking for it. Its smoothness, its spectrum and its ripples all match what a hot early universe should leave behind. No rival idea has explained all three.

words.d: the faint microwave glow from all directions, the cooled light of the early universe
a temperature scale that starts at absolute zero; 0 kelvin is minus 273 degrees Celsius
the coldest possible temperature, where particles have the least motion possible

look.title: The Hiss That Would Not Go Away
look.text: Two engineers point a giant horn antenna at the sky and hear a soft static. They aim it at a different patch: same static. They try at noon and at midnight, in summer and winter: same static. They scrub the horn clean and replace parts: same static, always the same strength.
look.prompt: What features of the hiss ruled out the sun, the city, or the equipment as its source, and pointed instead to the whole universe?

check.q: What is the cosmic microwave background?
choices: Light stretched from the hot early universe, now seen as microwaves
Radio noise from the sun
Heat from the center of our galaxy
Static from radio stations on Earth
check.why: It is the light released when the early universe cleared, redshifted by expansion into microwaves about 2.7 kelvin.

check.q: Why was finding the microwave background such strong evidence?
choices: It was the brightest thing in the sky
It had been predicted from the Big Bang idea before it was found
It proved that galaxies contain hydrogen
It showed the universe is not expanding
check.why: A prediction made in advance that is later confirmed is powerful evidence. The glow's temperature and spectrum matched expectations.

check.q: The tiny ripples in the microwave background are important because they:
choices: Show where the sun formed
Prove the universe has an edge
Are the seeds from which galaxies grew
Come from the pigeons in the antenna
check.why: Slightly denser spots in the early universe pulled in more matter over time. Those spots became galaxies and clusters.

lessons.title: How Old Is Everything
lessons.mainIdea: Independent evidence gives the universe an age of about 13.8 billion years and the sun and Earth about 4.6 billion.
reading: Light takes time to travel. Sunlight is about 8 minutes old when it reaches you. Light from the Andromeda galaxy left it about 2.5 million years ago. A *light-year* is the distance light travels in one year, roughly 9.5 trillion kilometers. So the farther out a telescope looks, the further back in time it sees. The James Webb telescope sees galaxies as they were more than 13 billion years ago.

Several lines of evidence agree on the universe's age. The expansion rate from Hubble's law, traced backward, gives a starting time. The ripples in the microwave background give an independent number. The oldest stars in our galaxy, dated by how they burn, are around 13 billion years old, and nothing found is older than the universe. All three point to about 13.8 billion years.

The Big Bang was not an explosion from a spot into empty space. Space itself has been stretching, everywhere at once. That is why every galaxy sees the others receding, with no center. Honest scientists also say what is not known. We do not know what, if anything, came before. We do not know why the expansion is speeding up, a discovery of 1998 that led to the name *dark energy* for whatever causes it.

Our own corner is much younger. The sun and the solar system formed about 4.6 billion years ago, when the universe was already two thirds of its present age. Earth's oldest surviving rocks are about 4 billion years old, and tiny zircon crystals in Australia reach about 4.4 billion years. The universe had been making galaxies, stars and heavy elements for 9 billion years before there was an Earth to stand on.

words.d: the distance light travels in one year, about 9.5 trillion kilometers
the name for whatever is causing the expansion of the universe to speed up; its nature is unknown
a tough mineral crystal that can survive for billions of years and be dated by radioactive decay

look.title: Raisin Bread Rising
look.text: A loaf of raisin bread dough sits in a warm oven and doubles in size in an hour. Two raisins that were 1 centimeter apart are now 2 centimeters apart. Two raisins that were 5 centimeters apart are now 10 centimeters apart. No raisin moved through the dough; the dough stretched.
look.prompt: From the view of any single raisin, how do the near and far raisins seem to move, and why does no raisin get to call itself the center?

check.q: Light from a galaxy 100 million light-years away shows the galaxy:
choices: As it is right now
As it will be in 100 million years
As it looked 100 years ago
As it was 100 million years ago
check.why: Light takes one year to cross one light-year. Light from 100 million light-years away has been traveling for 100 million years.

check.q: Which fact would contradict a 13.8-billion-year-old universe?
choices: A star reliably dated at 20 billion years old
A galaxy 12 billion light-years away
A planet older than the sun
A microwave background at 2.7 kelvin
check.why: Nothing can be older than the universe itself. A well-dated star older than 13.8 billion years would force scientists to rethink the age.

check.q: Why does every galaxy see all the others moving away from it?
choices: Our galaxy sits at the center of the universe
Space itself is stretching everywhere, so there is no center
Galaxies repel each other like magnets
Only the Milky Way is standing still
check.why: Like raisins in rising dough, every galaxy sees the others recede because the space between them grows. No point is the center.

lessons.title: A Cloud Becomes a Solar System
lessons.mainIdea: The sun and planets formed together from a collapsing, spinning cloud of gas and dust about 4.6 billion years ago.
reading: Look at how tidy the solar system is. All eight planets orbit the sun in the same direction, in nearly the same flat plane, in nearly circular paths. The sun spins the same way. Any explanation of the solar system has to account for this order. A pile of captured wanderers would not line up like that.

The accepted explanation is the *nebular hypothesis*, first sketched by Immanuel Kant in 1755 and Pierre-Simon Laplace in 1796. A cloud of gas and dust, a *nebula*, began to collapse under its own gravity, perhaps nudged by a nearby supernova. As it fell inward it spun faster, the way a skater spins faster pulling in her arms. Spinning flattened it into a disk with a fat, hot center. The center became the sun.

In the disk, dust grains stuck together into pebbles, then boulders, then bodies kilometers across. Gravity pulled these together in a process called *accretion*. Close to the young sun it was too hot for ice, so only rock and metal collected: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars. Farther out, past the frost line, ice was plentiful, and the cores that formed there grew large enough to pull in gas: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Leftovers became asteroids, comets and moons.

This is more than a story. Meteorites, the leftover crumbs, all date to about 4.56 billion years, giving the birthday. Since the 1990s telescopes have photographed flat disks around young stars, with dark gaps where planets are sweeping up material. In 2014 the ALMA radio telescope in Chile imaged the disk around the young star HL Tauri in stunning detail. We are watching other solar systems being born the way ours was.

words.d: a cloud of gas and dust in space, the raw material for stars and planets
the idea that the sun and planets formed from one collapsing, spinning cloud
the growth of a body as gravity pulls in and collects smaller pieces

look.title: The Spinning Skater
look.text: A figure skater spins slowly with her arms stretched wide. She pulls her arms in tight to her body and suddenly spins much faster, without pushing off the ice. A collapsing cloud thousands of times wider than the solar system does the same thing as gravity pulls it inward.
look.prompt: Why would a slowly turning cloud end up as a fast-spinning, flattened disk rather than a round ball, and what does that predict about the planets' orbits?

check.q: Which observation is best explained by the planets forming from one spinning disk?
choices: Planets have different colors
Jupiter has many moons
All planets orbit in the same direction in nearly the same plane
Earth has liquid water
check.why: A flat spinning disk gives every planet the same direction and plane. Captured objects would have random orbits.

check.q: Why are the inner planets rocky and the outer planets gas giants?
choices: The inner planets lost their gas to the solar wind recently
The sun pulled all the gas inward
The outer planets are older
Near the sun only rock and metal could condense; farther out, ice let cores grow big enough to hold gas
check.why: Temperature in the disk set what could solidify. Beyond the frost line, plentiful ice built large cores that captured hydrogen and helium.

check.q: What gives the solar system its age of about 4.6 billion years?
choices: Radioactive dating of meteorites
Counting the sun's spots
Measuring how far Pluto has drifted
The color of Jupiter's clouds
check.why: Meteorites are leftover pieces from the disk. Radioactive decay in them consistently gives about 4.56 billion years.

lessons.title: Kepler's Three Rules
lessons.mainIdea: Planets move on ellipses, speed up when nearer the sun, and take longer to orbit the farther out they are.
reading: For two thousand years astronomers assumed planets moved in perfect circles. The idea was beautiful, and it was wrong. In the late 1500s the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe measured planet positions with the best instruments before telescopes, night after night for decades. After Tycho died, Johannes Kepler took over his data on Mars. Kepler tried circle after circle. None fit. The errors were small, but Tycho's measurements were better than the errors, and Kepler refused to ignore them.

In 1609 Kepler published his first two rules. First, each planet moves on an *ellipse*, a stretched circle, with the sun at one of its two focus points, not at the center. Second, a planet moves faster when it is closer to the sun and slower when it is farther away. Kepler stated this exactly: a line from the sun to the planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times. Earth is nearest the sun in early January and moves fastest then.

Ten years later he found the third rule, the one that links the planets to each other. The farther a planet is from the sun, the longer its year, and in a precise way. The square of the *orbital period* equals the cube of the average distance. Here distance is measured in Earth-sun units and time in Earth years. Mars is about 1.5 times as far as Earth, and its year is about 1.9 Earth years. Jupiter at about 5.2 units takes almost 12 years.

Kepler described the motion but could not say why it happened. Isaac Newton did, in 1687. His law of *gravity* says every mass pulls every other mass, and the pull weakens with the square of the distance. From that one rule all three of Kepler's laws follow. The same law that makes an apple fall keeps Jupiter on its ellipse, and it lets NASA steer a spacecraft to a landing on Mars.

words.d: a stretched circle with two focus points; planetary orbits have this shape
the time a planet takes to go once around the sun
the attraction between all masses, which weakens with the square of the distance between them

look.title: Planets' Years
look.prompt: Saturn is about 9.5 times farther from the sun than Earth. Its year is about 29.5 Earth years. How does the third rule account for a year that grows so much faster than the distance?

check.q: Where is the sun in a planet's orbit?
choices: At the exact center of a circle
At one focus of an ellipse
At the edge of the orbit
Slightly outside the orbit
check.why: Kepler's first rule places the sun at one focus of the ellipse, not at the center. That is why a planet's distance from the sun changes.

check.q: When is a planet moving fastest along its orbit?
choices: When it is farthest from the sun
At the same speed everywhere
When it is closest to the sun
Only at the start of its year
check.why: The equal-areas rule means a planet must move faster when it is closer to the sun to sweep the same area in the same time.

check.q: A newly found planet orbits its star at 4 times Earth's distance from the sun. About how long is its year?
choices: About 4 years
About 2 years
About 16 years
About 8 years
check.why: Period squared equals distance cubed: 4 cubed is 64, and the square root of 64 is 8. So the year is about 8 Earth years.

lessons.title: Clocks in the Rocks
lessons.mainIdea: Radioactive atoms decay at steady, known rates, so the ratio of parent to daughter atoms in a rock tells its age.
reading: Some kinds of atoms are unstable. An atom of uranium-238, for example, will eventually break down through a chain of steps into lead-206. This is *radioactive decay*. You cannot predict when one atom will decay. But in a large group, the pattern is exact: after a fixed time, half of them will have decayed. That time is the *half-life*. After two half-lives, a quarter remain; after three, an eighth. Nothing known, not heat, pressure or chemistry, changes the rate.

That steadiness makes decay a clock. When a mineral crystal forms from molten rock, it locks in certain parent atoms and starts with almost no daughter atoms. As time passes, parents turn into daughters. Measure the ratio of the two in the crystal, know the half-life, and you can calculate how long ago the crystal formed. Different *isotopes* work for different timescales. Uranium-238, with a half-life of 4.47 billion years, dates the oldest rocks. Carbon-14, with a half-life of 5,730 years, dates bones and wood up to about 50,000 years old.

In the 1950s Clair Patterson at Caltech set out to date the Earth using uranium and lead. Lead contamination was everywhere, from pipes, paint and leaded gasoline, so he built one of the first ultra-clean laboratories. In 1956 he reported an age of about 4.55 billion years from meteorites, which formed with Earth from the same disk. Later work on lunar samples and the oldest zircon crystals agreed. The number has barely changed in seventy years.

The method is checked in many ways. Different parent-daughter pairs in the same rock give the same age. Layers of volcanic ash dated by decay fall in the right order in the rock record. Tree rings and yearly lake layers confirm carbon-14 for recent times. When independent clocks agree, confidence is high. Radioactive dating is why we can say, and not just guess, that Earth is about 4.5 billion years old.

words.d: the breakdown of an unstable atomic nucleus into a different, more stable one, releasing radiation
the time it takes for half of a group of radioactive atoms to decay
a form of an element whose atoms have a different number of neutrons, such as carbon-12 and carbon-14

look.title: Half-Lives of Dating Clocks
look.prompt: Why would carbon-14 be useless for dating a 2-billion-year-old rock, and why would rubidium-87 be a poor choice for a 10,000-year-old bone?

check.q: A rock contains one quarter of its original uranium-235. About how old is it?
choices: About 176 million years
About 704 million years
About 2.8 billion years
About 1.4 billion years
check.why: One quarter remaining means two half-lives have passed. Two times 704 million years is about 1.4 billion years.

check.q: Why did Patterson need an ultra-clean laboratory?
choices: Lead from everyday sources would contaminate the samples and give false ages
Uranium is dangerous to breathe
Meteorites must be kept cold
Dust would scratch the crystals
check.why: Lead was everywhere in the 1950s, from pipes to gasoline. Stray lead would change the parent-to-daughter ratio and ruin the measurement.

check.q: Which statement about half-lives is true?
choices: Heating a rock speeds up its decay
The decay rate stays the same no matter the conditions
Half-lives get shorter as atoms get older
Each atom decays at exactly the half-life
check.why: No known change in heat, pressure or chemistry alters a nucleus's decay rate. That constancy is what makes it a reliable clock.

review.q: What did Hubble's discovery of a Cepheid in Andromeda show?
choices: Andromeda is a separate galaxy far outside the Milky Way
Andromeda is a gas cloud inside the Milky Way
The Milky Way is the only galaxy
Cepheids exist only in Andromeda
review.why: The Cepheid's period gave its true brightness, and its faintness put it far beyond the Milky Way's edge.

review.q: Which tool lets astronomers know what a distant star is made of?
choices: Parallax
Its spectrum and absorption lines
Its orbital period
Its half-life
review.why: Each element absorbs a unique set of wavelengths, leaving a barcode of dark lines in the star's spectrum.

review.q: What is the sun's main energy source?
choices: Burning coal-like material
Slow gravitational shrinking
Fusion of hydrogen into helium in its core
Heat left over from its formation
review.why: Fusion converts a small fraction of mass into energy and can power the sun for about 10 billion years.

choices: They contain mostly red stars
Their light is filtered by dust
They are cooler than our galaxy
They are moving away from us as space expands
review.why: Motion away stretches light to longer wavelengths. Hubble found the shift grows with distance, the sign of expansion.

review.q: Which piece of evidence for the Big Bang was predicted before it was found?
choices: The cosmic microwave background
The rings of Saturn
The age of meteorites
The phases of Venus
review.why: Physicists predicted a leftover glow in 1948. Penzias and Wilson found it in 1964 as a uniform microwave hiss.

review.q: A star with 15 times the sun's mass will most likely:
choices: Live longer than the sun and become a white dwarf
Burn out quickly and end in a supernova
Never leave the main sequence
Become a red giant and then a planet
review.why: High mass means hotter, faster fusion and a short life. Stars above about eight solar masses end in supernovas.

review.q: Which observation supports the idea that the planets formed from one spinning disk?
choices: Mars is red
Some planets have rings
All planets orbit in the same direction in nearly one plane
The sun is much larger than the planets
review.why: A collapsing, spinning cloud flattens into a disk. Planets built from it share its direction and plane.

review.q: A mineral holds one eighth of its original potassium-40. Its half-life is 1.25 billion years. How old is the mineral?
choices: 1.25 billion years
2.5 billion years
10 billion years
3.75 billion years
review.why: One eighth remaining means three half-lives have passed. Three times 1.25 billion years is 3.75 billion years.
